title: The event loop
summary: How a single JavaScript thread serves many connections: the call stack, the microtask queue, the event loop phases, and why blocking code hurts every request.

sections.title: One thread, many waits
sections.body:
Node runs your JavaScript on **one thread**. It stays fast because most server work is waiting: for a socket, a disk read or a database reply. Node hands that waiting to the operating system (and a small thread pool, libuv, for file system, DNS lookups, compression and crypto) and keeps the JavaScript thread free.

When a wait finishes, a callback is queued. The **event loop** takes queued callbacks one at a time and runs each one to completion on the call stack. Nothing interrupts a running callback, so you never need locks around plain variables, but a callback that runs for 200 ms delays every other request by 200 ms.

sections.title: Phases of the loop
sections.body:
Each turn of the loop walks through phases in order:

1. **timers**: callbacks from `setTimeout` and `setInterval` whose time has passed.
2. **pending callbacks**: some deferred system errors.
3. **poll**: wait for and run I/O callbacks (sockets, files). The loop may block here when nothing else is due.
4. **check**: `setImmediate` callbacks.
5. **close callbacks**: for example a socket's `'close'` event.

A timer's delay is a **minimum**, not a promise: `setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs on a later turn, after the current callback and all microtasks.

sections.title: Microtasks run first
sections.body:
Between every callback, Node drains two queues before moving on: first the `process.nextTick` queue, then the **microtask** queue (promise reactions and `queueMicrotask`). Both are drained completely, including anything added while draining.

So the order for code started from the main script is: synchronous code, then `nextTick` callbacks, then promise callbacks, then timers and `setImmediate` on later phases. A recursive `nextTick` or a promise chain that never ends starves I/O, because the loop never gets back to the poll phase.
sections.code:
setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'), 0)
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('promise'))
queueMicrotask(() => console.log('microtask'))
console.log('sync')
// sync, promise, microtask, timeout

sections.title: Keeping the loop healthy
sections.body:
Signs of a blocked loop: latency rises for **all** routes at once, health checks time out, and CPU sits at 100% on one core. Common causes are large `JSON.parse`/`JSON.stringify` calls, synchronous APIs such as `readFileSync` inside a request, catastrophic regular expressions and tight loops over large arrays.

Fixes: stream or paginate large payloads, move CPU-heavy work to `worker_threads` or another service, split long loops into chunks with `setImmediate` between them, and measure event loop delay with `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay()`.

pitfalls: Calling synchronous file or crypto APIs inside a request handler.
Assuming `setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs before a resolved promise callback.
Recursive `process.nextTick` or microtask loops that starve I/O.
Believing `async` makes CPU-bound code run in parallel; it still runs on the one thread.

gotchas.question: What does this print?
gotchas.answer: A, D, C, B. Synchronous code runs first (A, D), then the microtask queue (C), then the timer on a later loop turn (B).
gotchas.code:
console.log('A')
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0)
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C'))
console.log('D')

gotchas.question: Is Node single-threaded?
gotchas.answer: Your JavaScript runs on one thread per process (or per worker). libuv keeps a thread pool, four threads by default, for file system work, DNS lookups, zlib and some crypto, and the OS handles network I/O asynchronously. So "single-threaded" describes your code, not the whole runtime.

gotchas.question: `setImmediate` or `setTimeout(fn, 0)`: which runs first?
gotchas.answer: From the main module the order is not guaranteed; it depends on how long process start-up took. Inside an I/O callback, `setImmediate` always runs first, because the check phase comes right after the poll phase.
